answer.headline: CY 2025 medium-hub gauge: median {F38} seats per departure
answer.body:
Across US airports stored as FAA hub class M, the CY 2025 distribution of average seats per departure (equal weight per airport) is P10 {F36}, P25 {F37}, P50 {F38}, P75 {F39}, and P90 {F40}. The interquartile range, P75 minus P25, is {F41}. The span from P10 to P90 is {F42}.

Each airport figure is {F38.class}: total seats divided by passenger departures on T-100 departing passenger and combi segments over {F38.period}. Percentiles use linear interpolation. {F36.definition}.

claims.text: For FAA hub class M in CY 2025, average seats per departure has P10 {F36}, P25 {F37}, median {F38}, P75 {F39}, and P90 {F40}.
The interquartile range of those airport-level averages is {F41}, and the P10-to-P90 span is {F42}.
The middle half of medium hubs lies between {F37} and {F39}. That spread describes gauge mix across airports; it does not establish fleet strategy, unmet demand, or profitability.

assumptions: Medium hub means the warehouse FAA hub class M on the airport record (latest ACAIS classification stored for that airport), not a hub class recomputed in this analysis from CY 2025 enplanements.
The distribution weights each airport equally. It is not weighted by departures, seats, or passengers.
The US set is the resolver group for hub class M, which includes state airports and SJU.
limitations: This is the distribution of airport-level average gauge, not the distribution of seats on individual departures.
The distribution operator returns P10, P25, P50, P75, and P90 only. Minimum, maximum, and histogram bins are not established here.
Cargo-only departures are outside the metric, which divides seats by passenger departures.
Terminal capacity, fares, unmet demand, and profitability are not measured by these data.
Hub class can differ from an informal medium-hub list if the stored ACAIS classification year is not CY 2025.
